findings.title: Create records storage failure as legacy duration
findings.body: In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recording the storage duration. Because recordLegacyDuration and recordStorageDuration are distinct Prometheus metrics, a storage-side failure will be misattributed to the legacy backend. Anyone alerting or graphing on legacy failures will see storage failures, and storage failures will be invisible. Use recordStorageDuration(true, ...) here.

findings.title: Update records storage failure as legacy duration
findings.body: In DualWriterMode3.Update, when d.Storage.Update fails the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration. Same effect as in Create: a unified-storage Update failure is reported as a legacy failure, silently corrupting the two latency/error time series. Use recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

findings.title: DeleteCollection async legacy call recorded as storage duration
findings.body: In the DeleteCollection async goroutine, the elapsed time of d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is fed to d.recordStorageDuration(...). Every other write path correctly uses recordLegacyDuration for the legacy leg; this one is mislabeled, so DeleteCollection legacy latency will be merged into the unified-storage histogram and the real legacy histogram will not see those calls.

findings.title: Async legacy Create inherits request context that is cancelled when the response returns
findings.body: The async Create goroutine derives its timeout from the inbound request context: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`. That ctx is the apiserver request context, which is cancelled as soon as the handler writes the response and returns. The whole purpose of mode 3 is to write to legacy "as a safe measure" after the request returns; here that guarantee is broken, and the legacy write will frequently be aborted by ctx.Done() before completing. Use a detached context (e.g., context.Background()) with the klog logger still attached.

findings.title: Async legacy Delete inherits request context
findings.body: Same problem as the Create goroutine on line 51: the Delete goroutine derives its context from the request context with WithTimeoutCause(... 10s). The legacy Delete will be cancelled when the apiserver request finishes, so the safety-net legacy delete is not guaranteed to run to completion.

findings.title: Async legacy Update inherits request context
findings.body: The async Update goroutine derives its context from the request context with WithTimeoutCause(... 10s). The legacy Update will be cancelled when the apiserver request finishes, so the safety-net legacy update is not guaranteed to run. The legacy store can therefore permanently diverge from unified storage on any request that finishes inside 10s.

findings.title: Async legacy DeleteCollection inherits request context
findings.body: Same as above: the DeleteCollection goroutine derives its context from the request context with WithTimeoutCause(... 10s), so the legacy bulk delete will be cancelled when the handler returns and the two stores will diverge.

findings.title: Async legacy Create uses the pre-storage object, not the stored object
findings.body: After d.Storage.Create succeeds, the returned `created` object contains the UID, resourceVersion, creation timestamp, etc. that unified storage assigned. The async goroutine calls d.Legacy.Create with the original `obj` parameter instead, so the legacy store never sees the metadata assigned by storage (or assigns its own), producing two records with different identities for what should be the same resource. The legacy record is effectively orphaned from the unified one.

findings.title: Async legacy Update re-evaluates UpdatedObjectInfo against legacy's current state
findings.body: The async Update goroutine passes the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update. UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is called inside the legacy store against whatever it currently holds, not against the state storage just wrote. The previous implementation wrapped objInfo around the resolved object and passed the same wrapped value to both stores so they would apply identical changes; here the legacy store can compute and persist a different version, causing legacy and storage to diverge.

findings.title: Mode3 doc comment describes the wrong write order
findings.body: The comment on newDualWriterMode3 says "Mode 3 represents writing to LegacyStorage and Storage and reading from Storage." The actual behavior implemented below is: write synchronously to Storage, then fire-and-forget an asynchronous write to LegacyStorage, and read only from Storage. The comment therefore misleads readers about both the ordering and the async nature of mode 3.

findings.title: Delete success path labels metric with name instead of Kind
findings.body: On successful d.Storage.Delete, d.recordStorageDuration is called with `name` as the kind label, while every other path (and the failing branch on line 103) uses options.Kind. As a result, the storage latency histogram for Delete will be tagged with the resource name instead of the resource kind, breaking grouping with all other operations.

findings.title: TestMode3_Create never asserts that the legacy async Create actually ran
findings.body: TestMode3_Create registers an expectation on the legacy store mock via setupLegacyFn but the goroutine that should satisfy it is never synchronized with (no wait, no channel, no AssertExpectations). The test currently passes even if the legacy async write is removed or short-circuited, so the very behavior mode 3 introduces - the legacy safety-net write - is effectively untested.

findings.title: TestMode3_Update never asserts the legacy async Update ran
findings.body: TestMode3_Update registers a mock expectation for legacy Update but does not synchronize with or assert against the async goroutine. The same problem as Create: the legacy safety-net update is not actually verified.

findings.title: TestMode3_DeleteCollection has no legacy setup or assertion at all
findings.body: The testCase struct does not include setupLegacyFn and no mock expectation is registered for d.Legacy.DeleteCollection. The implementation runs an async legacy DeleteCollection but nothing in this test exercises it - the safety-net behavior on the bulk-delete path is entirely uncovered.

findings.title: TestMode3_Get does not verify legacy Get is never called
findings.body: Mode 3 reads must come from storage only, but TestMode3_Get never asserts that the legacy store is not called (the analogous TestMode1_Get uses us.AssertNotCalled on Delete). A future change that accidentally adds a legacy Get would not be caught.

findings.title: TestMode3_Get uses a local prometheus registry while the rest of the file uses the package-level p
findings.body: All other tests in dualwriter_mode3_test.go and dualwriter_mode1_test.go use the package-level `p`; TestMode3_Get creates its own `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` inside the test body, masking the global and being a leftover from before the global existed. Minor, but should be aligned.
